# You're inside a real Lantern workspace

This whole thing is running in your browser. No install, no account, nothing saved to a server. It's a pretend matter for a solo attorney, pre-loaded so you can actually poke around instead of staring at an empty screen.

Everything here is a real Lantern surface. The files are real files. The editor is the real editor. The AI sidebar talks to a real model.

## What to try

1. Open `Halvorsen Estate/Deposition Notes.md` and read the notes the way an attorney actually keeps them.
2. Open `Halvorsen Estate/Deposition contradictions.aichat` to watch a saved AI conversation play back, the kind that finds where a witness said two different things.
3. Open the AI sidebar and ask it something about the open file. The demo uses a shared, rate-limited key.
4. Hit a limit? Paste your own Anthropic key for unlimited use, or download the app.

Here's the part that matters. On your own machine, these files live in a folder you pick, and your API key goes straight from your computer to the model. Nothing routes through a server I control. That's the whole point of Lantern, and it's why an attorney can use it on a live matter.

Refresh the page and the workspace comes back to where it started.

# Deposition Notes: Markus Halvorsen

**Matter:** Halvorsen Estate v. Cedar Point Holdings, LLC
**Deponent:** Markus Halvorsen (defendant, managing member)
**Date:** April 14, 2026
**Reporter:** present, transcript pending

Rough notes taken during the deposition. Page cites are to the realtime feed, confirm against the certified transcript when it comes back.

## Background he gave

Halvorsen ran Cedar Point as managing member from 2019 to the sale in late 2024. Says the accountant handled "all the numbers" and he mostly signed what was put in front of him.

## Testimony to remember

- **p. 12** Asked whether he saw the second appraisal before the sale closed. Answer: "No. I never saw a second appraisal. The first one was the only number I had."
- **p. 31** On the timeline: says the sale closed "sometime in November, I think the 20th or so."
- **p. 47** Asked what documents he reviewed before closing. Answer: "I reviewed all the paperwork the accountant sent over. The appraisals, the title work, the closing statement. All of it."
- **p. 52** Says he and the accountant "talked every week without fail" during the sale.
- **p. 68** Says he was "traveling most of October and November" and "hard to reach."

## My flags during the read

- p. 12 vs p. 47 looks like a straight contradiction on the second appraisal. Pull Exhibit 9 (the appraisal transmittal email) and check the date.
- p. 52 vs p. 68 is softer: "talked every week without fail" against "traveling and hard to reach" for the same two months. Worth a follow-up.
- Nail down the closing date (p. 31, "the 20th or so") against the recorded deed.

## To do

- Run these against the full transcript when it lands.
- Cross-reference the exhibit list.
- Draft follow-up questions for the second session.

# Privilege Log: Halvorsen Estate v. Cedar Point Holdings

Working draft. Each withheld document gets a row. Descriptions are written so they identify the document without revealing the legal advice itself.

| Date | Author | Recipient | Type | Privilege | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-09-02 | Client | Me | Email | Attorney-Client | Client request for advice regarding appraisal discrepancy |
| 2024-09-03 | Me | Client | Email | Attorney-Client | Counsel's response analyzing options |
| 2024-10-11 | Me | (file) | Memo | Work Product | Internal analysis of exposure prepared in anticipation of litigation |
| 2024-11-04 | Client | Me | Email | Attorney-Client | Client questions ahead of closing |

Notes:

- The 2024-10-11 memo is work product, not attorney-client, because it was prepared for the file in anticipation of litigation, not sent to the client. Keep the basis straight per entry.
- Do not let a description reveal the substance of the advice. "Analyzing options" is fine. The actual options are not.
- Confirm the column format against the local rule before producing.

# Case Timeline: Halvorsen Estate v. Cedar Point Holdings

Built from the documents and the deposition notes. Dates in brackets are unconfirmed and need a source.

- **2019-03** Halvorsen becomes managing member of Cedar Point.
- **2024-08-15** First appraisal delivered ($4.2M).
- **[2024-09-01]** Second appraisal commissioned. Source needed. Halvorsen denies seeing this (Depo p. 12).
- **2024-09-02** Client emails counsel about the appraisal discrepancy (see Privilege Log).
- **[2024-11-20]** Sale closes. Halvorsen said "the 20th or so" (Depo p. 31). Confirm against the recorded deed.
- **2025-02** Estate files suit.
- **2026-04-14** Halvorsen deposition, first session.

## Open dates to confirm

- The second-appraisal commission date. This is the hinge of the p. 12 / p. 47 contradiction.
- The exact closing date.

# Client Intake Summary

**Client:** Estate of Anders Halvorsen (represented by the executor)
**Adverse party:** Cedar Point Holdings, LLC; Markus Halvorsen, managing member
**Matter type:** Civil, business dispute arising from a 2024 sale
**Date opened:** 2025-01-20

## What the client wants

The estate believes the company was sold below value because a second, higher appraisal was set aside before closing. They want to know whether that was concealment and what recovery looks like.

## Conflict check

Ran the names through the system. No conflict with current or former clients. (This template does not perform the check for you, it reminds you to do it and records that you did.)

## Key facts to verify

- Whether a second appraisal existed and when.
- Who saw it before closing.
- The actual closing date and sale price.

## Statute of limitations

Flag: confirm the limitations period for the underlying claim and calendar it. Do not rely on this note for the date.

# About this demo

This is the in-browser version of Lantern. It runs the same editor, file tree, and AI chat the desktop app uses, just pre-loaded with a fictional matter so you have something to look at.

The matter, the names, and the facts are all made up for illustration. Nothing here is legal advice, and the AI's job in the real app is to produce a first draft you review, not to practice law.

What's different from the real app: this demo uses a shared, rate-limited key so you can try the AI without setting anything up. On your own machine you bring your own key (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, or a local model through Ollama), and your files and your key never leave your computer.

When you're ready, download the 30-day trial at advisorprephero.com.
